title: Iron, Farming and Movement
description: Nok sculpture and early iron, the Bantu expansion, and Jenné-jeno's city without kings

concepts.title: Nok: Terracottas and Early Iron
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1928 tin miners near the village of Nok in central Nigeria pulled a small terracotta head out of mining gravels. In the 1940s the archaeologist Bernard Fagg recognized it, along with a head a mine clerk had been using as a scarecrow in a yam field, as the work of an ancient culture he named Nok. The sculptures are human figures and heads, some near life size, with elaborate hairstyles and triangular or D-shaped eyes with pierced pupils.

The dates have moved. A long-running Goethe University Frankfurt project led by Peter Breunig, using radiocarbon dates on plant remains, places the first Nok settlements around 1500 BCE, the sculptures from about 900 BCE, and the culture's end in the last centuries BCE; older estimates ran into the first centuries CE. The project also excavated iron-smelting furnaces in the Nok region dating to around the middle of the first millennium BCE, among the earliest in West Africa.

Where African iron smelting began is still debated. Some archaeologists argue for independent invention south of the Sahara; others think the knowledge came from North Africa or the Nile. Very early claims, such as dates near 1500 BCE from the Termit massif in Niger, are contested partly because the charcoal dated may be older than the furnace. Most agree on one thing: over much of sub-Saharan Africa people went from stone tools to iron with no long bronze age in between.

Looting has damaged the evidence. Since the 1990s demand from the art market has fueled heavy looting, so most Nok pieces in collections don't have a record of where they were found, and fakes circulate.

concepts.title: The Bantu Expansion: Three Kinds of Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
From Cameroon to South Africa, around 500 closely related Bantu languages are spoken (counts vary with how dialects are split), among them Swahili, Kikongo, Shona, Zulu and Xhosa. The linguist Wilhelm Bleek named the group in 1862 from a widespread word for "people", bantu. Shared grammar built on noun classes, and shared vocabulary, point to one ancestor language. Bantu languages are most diverse near the Nigeria–Cameroon border, and because language families tend to be most varied where they have been spoken longest, linguists place the homeland there.

Archaeology tracks villages, pottery and crops. Farming communities spread south through and around the equatorial rainforest. By about 500 BCE Urewe pottery and ironworking appear around Lake Victoria, and farming villages reached what is now KwaZulu-Natal by the middle of the first millennium CE. Iron is no longer seen as the engine of the spread, since it began before these speakers had iron; iron later moved along routes already open. Older textbooks pictured iron-armed conquerors, while current work describes a long, uneven spread over more than three thousand years.

Genetics adds dates and routes. A 2024 study in Nature led by Cesar Fortes-Lima, which sampled more than 1,500 Bantu speakers, dates the start of the expansion to roughly 6,000 to 4,000 years ago in western Africa.1 Several studies since 2017 favor a "late split", in which speakers first moved south through the rainforest and the eastern branch separated later, south of it. Genomes also show heavy mixing with earlier foragers and herders, and language records the same contact: the click consonants of Xhosa and Zulu were borrowed from Khoe-San languages.

concepts.title: Jenné-jeno: A City Without a Citadel
concepts.contentHtml:
Jenné-jeno ("ancient Djenné") is a mound about 3 km from the modern town of Djenné in Mali's Inland Niger Delta, a floodplain rich in fish, rice and pasture. Susan and Roderick McIntosh excavated it in 1977 and 1981. People settled there around 250 BCE. The town grew through the first millennium CE, was ringed by a mud-brick wall around 800 CE, declined after about 1100 and was largely abandoned by about 1400. Population estimates vary widely.

The floodplain has no stone and no iron ore, yet the earliest levels contain iron and stone brought from tens of kilometers away, and later levels hold copper and glass beads from distant sources. This regional trade was running centuries before Arab merchants began crossing the Sahara in the 8th century. It undercut a colonial-era assumption that West African towns were created by North African traders.

What you won't find at Jenné-jeno matters as much. Excavators didn't find a palace, a monumental temple, rich royal tombs or a walled elite quarter. Instead the town sat at the center of an urban cluster of dozens of smaller mounds within a few kilometers, which the McIntoshes read as communities of specialists, such as smiths, potters, fishers and herders, living close together yet apart. Susan McIntosh and others call this heterarchy, meaning power spread among several groups that balanced one another, with no single ruler at the top.

Critics note that only a small part of the site has been excavated, so the missing elites may simply be missing evidence. That makes the model an interpretation.

title: Kush and Aksum
description: Nubian kingdoms from Kerma to Meroë, and the Red Sea power of Aksum

concepts.title: Kerma, Napata and the Kushite Pharaohs
concepts.contentHtml:
The Nile valley south of Egypt, called Kush in Egyptian texts and Nubia by later writers, produced Africa's earliest states outside Egypt. At Kerma, near the Third Cataract in today's Sudan, a kingdom flourished from about 2500 to 1500 BCE. Its rulers built the Western Deffufa, a massive mud-brick temple, and were buried under great earthen mounds, some with dozens or even hundreds of sacrificed attendants, as George Reisner's excavations of 1913 to 1916 revealed. Kerma raided Egypt during Egypt's period of division before about 1550 BCE, and Egyptian armies under Thutmose I destroyed it around 1500 BCE.1 Egypt then ruled Nubia for more than four centuries.

After Egyptian rule ended, a new Kushite kingdom arose at Napata, beside Jebel Barkal, a flat-topped mountain sacred to the god Amun. Around 728 BCE King Piye marched north and conquered Egypt;2 his victory stela at Jebel Barkal tells the story. His successors ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty. Taharqa (r. 690 to 664 BCE), who appears in the Hebrew Bible as Tirhakah, built at Karnak and Jebel Barkal. The Kushite kings presented themselves as restorers of old Egyptian piety and revived pyramid burial at el-Kurru and Nuri.

Their rule in Egypt ended under Assyrian attack: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BCE, and Ashurbanipal's army sacked Thebes in 663 BCE, driving out Tantamani. The evidence for this period is unusually varied: royal inscriptions in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Assyrian annals, the Bible, and Herodotus, who wrote of a king "Sabacos" (Shabaka).

concepts.title: Meroë: Iron, Pyramids and the Kandakes
concepts.contentHtml:
After an Egyptian army sacked Napata in 593 BCE, the center of Kush shifted south to Meroë, where royal burials begin around 270 BCE; the Meroitic period ran to about 350 CE. Meroë's slag heaps led A. H. Sayce, early in the 20th century, to call it the "Birmingham of Africa", and older books claimed ironworking spread from there across Africa. That view has collapsed: iron in West and Central Africa is as early or earlier. Recent work led by Jane Humphris shows smelting at Meroë from at least the 7th or 6th century BCE, lasting over a thousand years.

Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, over 200, at el-Kurru, Nuri, Jebel Barkal and Meroë. They are smaller and steeper, with burial chambers cut beneath. Many at Meroë lost their tops in 1834 to the Italian treasure hunter Giuseppe Ferlini.

The Meroitic script has a hieroglyphic and a cursive form of 23 signs each. F. Ll. Griffith worked out their sound values around 1909 to 1911, using royal names written in both Meroitic and Egyptian. Scholars can read the texts aloud but understand little, because no long bilingual text exists. Claude Rilly has argued, and many specialists accept, that the language belongs to the Northern East Sudanic branch of Nilo-Saharan.

Kandake (Greek and Latin Candace) was a title of royal women; some ruled in their own right. Strabo describes a one-eyed "Candace", usually identified as Amanirenas, whose army raided Roman Egypt around 25 BCE. After Roman counterattacks her envoys reached Augustus, who dropped his tribute demand. A bronze head of Augustus was found in 1910 buried under temple steps at Meroë.

concepts.title: Aksum: Coins, Stelae and a Christian King
concepts.contentHtml:
Aksum, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a major power from about the 1st to the 7th century CE. Its Red Sea port, Adulis, linked Roman Egypt, South Arabia and India. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide from the 1st century CE, names Adulis and a ruler called Zoskales and lists exports of ivory, tortoiseshell and rhinoceros horn.

From around 270 CE, under King Endubis, Aksum minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze, a rare step then; gold coins carried Greek legends.1 Elite tombs were marked by granite stelae carved to look like multistory buildings, with false doors and windows. The largest, about 33 meters long, lies broken, probably having fallen during or soon after erection. A 24-meter stele taken to Rome by Italian troops in 1937 was returned in 2005 and re-erected in 2008.

King Ezana's inscriptions, in Ge'ez, Greek and South Arabian script, record a religious turn around the 330s or 340s. Early texts call him son of Mahrem, a war god; later ones invoke the "Lord of Heaven", and a Greek inscription names Father, Son and Holy Spirit. His coins replace the old crescent and disc with a cross. The church historian Rufinus (c. 400) tells of Frumentius, a Syrian Christian captive who rose at court and was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria; scholars debate the details. The Ethiopian church depended on Alexandria for its head bishops until 1959.

A Coptic Manichaean text, the Kephalaia, attributes to the Persian prophet Mani (died 274 or 277) a list of the world's four great kingdoms: Babylon and Persia, Rome, Aksum, and probably China.

title: Ghana: Gold, Salt and the Sahara
description: How trans-Saharan trade worked, what al-Bakri reported, and the Almoravid debate

concepts.title: Gold, Salt and Camels
concepts.contentHtml:
Trans-Saharan trade rested on an imbalance. The savanna and forest zones of West Africa had gold but little salt; the Sahara had salt but needed grain; North Africa and the Mediterranean wanted gold for coinage.1 The main gold fields were Bambuk, between the Senegal and Falémé rivers, and later Bure, on the upper Niger. They lay largely beyond Ghana's direct rule: Ghana grew rich by controlling and taxing the trade. Northbound caravans also carried ivory and enslaved people, a traffic that lasted for centuries. Southbound came salt, copper, horses, cloth, glass beads and, later, books and paper.

The camel made regular crossings practical. Dromedaries spread across North Africa during the Roman period, and caravan trade grew from about the 3rd to 5th centuries CE. After the Arab conquest of North Africa, merchants based in towns such as Sijilmasa, founded in southern Morocco in the 8th century, organized it on a larger scale. A crossing took about two months.

Ibn Battuta, who crossed in 1352, described the salt mine of Taghaza in the western Sahara: a village whose houses and mosque were built of salt blocks roofed with camel skins, without a tree in sight, where enslaved workers cut the slabs that camels carried south. Salt was worth hauling because people and herds in hot climates need it and the Sahel had few good sources.

Some stories need caution. The "silent trade", in which partners exchanged goods without ever meeting, appears in Herodotus about Carthaginian traders and recurs in later Arabic writing. It is better read as a travelers' motif than as a reliable description.

concepts.title: Al-Bakri's Ghana
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval Ghana, which its Soninke people called Wagadu, lay in the Sahel of today's southern Mauritania and western Mali, far northwest of modern Ghana. The modern country borrowed the name at independence in 1957; there is no direct link. Arabic writers mention Ghana from the late 8th century, when the astronomer al-Fazari called it the land of gold. Arabic geographies and local oral traditions are the central evidence for medieval West Africa, and both need careful reading.

The fullest account comes from al-Bakri, a geographer in Córdoba who finished his Book of Routes and Realms in 1068. He never visited West Africa; he compiled reports from merchants and earlier writers, so his rich detail is secondhand. He explains that "Ghana" was the title of the king. The capital, he says, was two towns six miles apart: a Muslim town with twelve mosques and resident scholars, and the king's town, with his palace, domed houses and sacred groves where priests guarded the royal tombs. The king, Tunka Manin in 1063, followed the local religion but employed Muslim ministers and interpreters.1 Succession passed to the king's sister's son.

Al-Bakri also records royal policy. The king took one gold dinar for each donkey-load of salt entering the country and two dinars for each load leaving. All gold nuggets belonged to him and only gold dust was left to the people, so that gold would not become so plentiful that it lost its value.

Ruins at Koumbi Saleh in southeastern Mauritania, excavated since 1914, include stone houses and a large mosque. Many identify them with al-Bakri's Muslim town, but this is not proven, and the king's town has never been securely located.

concepts.title: The Almoravid Question
concepts.contentHtml:
The Almoravids (al-Murabitun) began in the 1040s as a reform movement among Sanhaja Berbers of the western Sahara, led by the preacher Abd Allah ibn Yasin. In 1054 to 1055 they seized Sijilmasa and sacked Awdaghust, a southern trading town that, al-Bakri reports, had submitted to Ghana. A northern wing under Yusuf ibn Tashfin conquered Morocco and much of al-Andalus; a southern wing under Abu Bakr ibn Umar stayed in the Sahara until his death in 1087.

Many 20th-century textbooks say the Almoravids stormed Ghana's capital in 1076 and destroyed the empire. The written basis is thin. The geographer al-Zuhri, writing in the 12th century, says the people of Ghana became Muslims in 1076 to 1077, which records a conversion, not a conquest. Ibn Khaldun, writing three centuries later, says Almoravid pressure weakened Ghana and that neighbors then overran it.

In two articles of 1982 and 1983, David Conrad and Humphrey Fisher called it "the conquest that never was". No contemporary source describes a military conquest;1 al-Idrisi, writing in 1154, still calls Ghana the largest and most commercial town of the Sudan, under a Muslim king; and local oral traditions recall no Almoravid sack. They proposed peaceful conversion and alliance. Critics such as Sheryl Burkhalter replied that Almoravid control of the gold flow implies real political leverage. Many historians now favor influence and conversion over a sack, but the question stays open.

Ghana faded in the 12th and 13th centuries as gold sources and routes shifted east. Oral tradition says the Sosso king Sumaguru Kanté took its remnant around 1200, and Soninke legend blames the killing of Bida, a serpent who guarded Wagadu, for drought and dispersal.

title: Mali and Songhai
description: Sundiata's epic, Mansa Musa's pilgrimage, Timbuktu's scholars and the fall of Songhai

concepts.title: Sundiata and the Griots
concepts.contentHtml:
The empire of Mali grew from Manden, the Mande heartland on the upper Niger near today's Guinea–Mali border. Its founder, Sundiata Keita (also Sunjata or Son-Jara), defeated Sumaguru Kanté of Sosso at the battle of Kirina, traditionally dated around 1235, a date worked back from later records.

Sundiata is known mainly through the epic that bears his name, performed by jeliw (singular jeli; in French, griots), hereditary bards who keep genealogies, praise songs and history for patron families. In the best-known version Sundiata, son of Sogolon, cannot walk as a child, rises dramatically, goes into exile and returns to face the sorcerer-king Sumaguru, whose protective magic fails once his secret weakness, the spur of a white cockerel, is discovered. That version is Djibril Tamsir Niane's French prose of 1960, based on the performance of the jeli Mamadou Kouyaté and translated into English in 1965. Other recorded versions, such as Fa-Digi Sisòkò's, differ in many details.

Historians use the epic carefully. Oral traditions carry memory over centuries but also compress time, merge characters, add later Islamic elements and flatter the lineages that sponsor them. Independent checks help. Ibn Khaldun, writing in the late 14th century from informants, names Mari Jata as the Mali king who conquered Sosso, which supports the epic's core. A "Manden Charter" said to have been proclaimed by Sundiata's assembly at Kurukan Fuga was written down from oral recitation in 1998 and listed by UNESCO in 2009; historians treat that text as a modern compilation drawing on older traditions.

Even Mali's capital is uncertain: Niani in Guinea was long proposed, but excavations there did not confirm it.

concepts.title: Mansa Musa and the Outsiders' Accounts
concepts.contentHtml:
Mansa Musa ruled Mali from about 1312 to 1337; the dates are uncertain.1 In 1324 he passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca with a large retinue and much gold. The fullest account is by al-Umari, a Mamluk official who wrote about twelve years later from what Cairo officials and merchants told him; he was not an eyewitness. He reports that Musa at first refused to prostrate himself before the sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, gave gold freely, and by the end had to borrow from Cairo merchants. Before the visit, al-Umari says, a mithqal of gold never fetched less than 25 silver dirhams; afterward it fetched no more than 22, and was still depressed twelve years on. These figures come from one writer and cannot be checked.

Modern claims that Musa was the richest person who ever lived, often with a dollar figure attached, come from internet lists of the 2010s. They are unmeasurable: a king's control of gold flows and tribute is not a personal fortune, and no figures survive to convert. Musa returned with scholars and the Andalusian poet al-Sahili, traditionally credited with designing Timbuktu's Djinguereber mosque, rebuilt many times since.

The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta reached the Mali capital in 1352 and stayed into 1353, under Musa's brother Mansa Sulayman. In his Rihla, dictated to the scholar Ibn Juzayy in Fez, he praises the complete safety of travel, the crowds at Friday prayer and the children made to memorize the Quran. He condemns servant women going unclothed in public, subjects throwing dust on their heads before the king, and a welcome gift he thought stingy. His verdicts reflect his own standards as a Muslim jurist.

concepts.title: Songhai, Timbuktu and Tondibi
concepts.contentHtml:
Timbuktu began around 1100 as a Tuareg seasonal camp, according to the 17th-century chronicle Tarikh al-Sudan. It became a center of Islamic learning, with scholars teaching circles at the Sankore and Djinguereber mosques rather than in one university. Djenné had its own scholars; its Great Mosque was rebuilt in 1907 on the site of an older one.

Songhai, based at Gao, broke away from Mali and expanded under Sunni Ali (r. 1464 to 1492), who took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné around 1473. The Tarikh al-Sudan, written by the Timbuktu scholar al-Sa'di in the 1650s, portrays him as a tyrant who persecuted Timbuktu's scholars; Songhai oral tradition remembers a mighty magician-king. Askia Muhammad (r. 1493 to 1528), a general who seized power, made the hajj in 1496 to 1497 and consulted the North African jurist al-Maghili on governing. Songhai became the largest West African state of its time.

In 1590 Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco sent Judar Pasha, a Spanish-born convert, across the Sahara with about 4,000 men, most armed with arquebuses, plus cannon. On 13 March 1591 at Tondibi, near Gao, they routed the army of Askia Ishaq II. Al-Sa'di gives the Songhai 12,500 cavalry and 30,000 infantry; the numbers are unreliable, but the Songhai clearly had far more men and almost no firearms. Morocco occupied Gao and Timbuktu and deported the scholar Ahmad Baba to Marrakesh.

Timbuktu's family libraries hold manuscripts estimated in the hundreds of thousands, on law, theology, astronomy and medicine, but most surviving copies date from the 16th to 19th centuries. During the jihadist occupation of 2012 to 2013 some were burned and many more were smuggled to Bamako.

title: The Swahili Coast and the Zimbabwe Plateau
description: Monsoon trade, coral-stone towns and the African builders of Great Zimbabwe

concepts.title: Stone Towns of the Swahili Coast
concepts.contentHtml:
From southern Somalia to northern Mozambique, a chain of trading towns grew from the 8th century onward: Shanga, Lamu, Pate, Malindi, Mombasa, Zanzibar, Kilwa and others. Early houses were of timber and mud. From about the 11th century, wealthy townspeople built in coral stone set in lime mortar, raising mosques, tombs and many-roomed houses.

Kilwa Kisiwani, an island town in southern Tanzania, became the richest by the 13th and 14th centuries, when it controlled the gold trade passing through Sofala, in Mozambique, from the Zimbabwe plateau. It minted its own copper coins. Its Great Mosque, begun around the 11th century, was enlarged with domes in the 14th, and the sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulayman built the vast palace of Husuni Kubwa above the sea. Ibn Battuta, visiting about 1331, called Kilwa one of the most beautiful and best-built towns in the world.1

Colonial-era writers treated these towns as Arab or Persian colonies. Archaeology since the 1980s shows otherwise: local pottery traditions run continuously from the earliest levels, and stone houses developed from local forms. Swahili is a Bantu language, with Bantu grammar and noun classes, that absorbed many Arabic words. These were African towns that adopted Islam.

Ancestry is a related but separate question. Kilwa's 16th-century chronicle claims founders from Shiraz in Persia, long read as a prestige myth. A 2023 ancient DNA study led by Esther Brielle, of people buried in coastal towns between about 1250 and 1800, found that many had substantial Asian ancestry, mainly from Persian and Indian men, and African ancestry mainly from women, with mixing from about 1000 CE. The language and much of the culture stayed African.

concepts.title: Riding the Monsoon
concepts.contentHtml:
The Indian Ocean monsoon set the coast's calendar. Roughly from November to March the northeast monsoon carried ships from Arabia, the Persian Gulf and western India toward East Africa; roughly from April to September the southwest monsoon carried them home. A merchant could make one round trip a year and often waited months in port, lodging with local hosts, which fostered partnerships and marriages between visiting traders and coastal families. The pattern is old: the 1st-century Periplus already describes a market town called Rhapta on this coast, though its site has never been found.

East Africa exported gold, ivory, ambergris, tortoiseshell, rock crystal, mangrove poles for building in the treeless Gulf, and enslaved people. Enslaved Africans called Zanj in Arabic, many probably from East Africa, rose in the Zanj Rebellion in southern Iraq from 869 to 883. Imports included cotton cloth from Gujarat, glass beads, glazed pottery from Persia and Chinese porcelain. Chinese celadon and blue-and-white wares turn up all along the coast, some set into the walls of mosques and pillar tombs as decoration, along with Chinese coins.

Most Chinese goods arrived through Indian and Arabian middlemen; direct contact was brief. The Ming fleets of the admiral Zheng He visited Mogadishu, Barawa and Malindi on voyages between 1417 and 1422. Shortly before, in 1414 and 1415, giraffes from East Africa reached the Ming court, one brought by envoys from Malindi, and were hailed as the auspicious qilin. The voyages ended in the 1430s.

The next outsiders came to take control. Vasco da Gama reached Mombasa and Malindi in 1498, and in 1505 Portuguese forces sacked Kilwa and Mombasa in a bid to seize the gold trade.

concepts.title: Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe
concepts.contentHtml:
At Mapungubwe, near where South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe meet, a farming community settled at a site called K2 in the 11th century and moved its elite onto Mapungubwe Hill by about 1220. Rulers lived above commoners, an early clear case of class separation in southern Africa. Hilltop graves excavated in the 1930s held gold objects, including a small rhinoceros of gold foil over a wooden core, with glass beads and Chinese celadon from coastal trade. The hill was abandoned around 1290 to 1300, perhaps as conditions grew drier, and power moved north.

Great Zimbabwe, near modern Masvingo, flourished from about the 11th to the 15th century, with most stone building in the 13th to 15th. Its Hill Complex and Great Enclosure are built of granite blocks laid without mortar; the Enclosure's outer wall runs about 250 meters around and stands up to about 11 meters high. Carved soapstone birds were found there. Wealth came from cattle and from control of gold exports: excavators found a copper coin of a Kilwa sultan, Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain. Power later shifted to the Mutapa state in the north and to Khami in the west.

The builders were ancestors of Shona speakers, but white colonists refused to accept it. Karl Mauch in 1871 linked the ruins to the Queen of Sheba, and Theodore Bent in 1891 to Phoenicians or Arabs. David Randall-MacIver concluded in 1905 that they were medieval and African, and Gertrude Caton-Thompson confirmed it in 1929. Rhodesia's white-minority government still pressed for official vagueness, and the archaeologist Peter Garlake left the country in 1970 after government opposition. In 1980 independent Zimbabwe took its name from the site.

title: Forest and Highland Kingdoms
description: Ife and Benin, Lalibela and the Solomonic kings, Kongo and Kanem-Bornu

concepts.title: Ife and Benin: Brass, Clay and Earth
concepts.contentHtml:
Ile-Ife, in southwestern Nigeria, is the sacred city where, in Yoruba tradition, the world was created and the first king, Oduduwa, ruled.1 Between about the 12th and 15th centuries its artists made strikingly naturalistic heads in terracotta and in copper alloys, cast by the lost-wax method. When the German ethnographer Leo Frobenius found a head at Ife in 1910, he credited it to a lost Atlantis linked to the ancient Greeks. More heads unearthed at the Wunmonije compound in 1938 helped establish them as Yoruba work.

The kingdom of Benin, of the Edo people of today's southern Nigeria (not the modern Republic of Benin, formerly Dahomey), expanded in the 15th century under Oba Ewuare, according to oral tradition. Its brass casters, organized in the royal guild Igun Eronmwon, made heads, figures and, mainly in the 16th and 17th centuries, rectangular plaques showing obas, chiefs, warriors and Portuguese traders. Much of their metal came from brass manillas, ring-shaped currency imported by Europeans. Around and beyond the city run banks and ditches, the iya, which Patrick Darling estimated in the 1970s at about 16,000 km in total, dug over centuries, perhaps from the 8th to the 15th.

In January 1897 a British party led by the acting consul-general James Phillips, traveling to Benin City although the oba had asked for a delay, was ambushed and most were killed. In February a British force took the city, burned much of it and carried off thousands of brass, ivory and wooden objects, many sold to cover costs. Oba Ovonramwen was exiled to Calabar. Since 2022 several museums, notably in Germany, have returned ownership of some objects to Nigeria.

concepts.title: Ethiopia: Lalibela and the Solomonic Kings
concepts.contentHtml:
Christian kingship in the Ethiopian highlands outlived Aksum. By the 12th century the Zagwe dynasty, Agaw-speaking rulers whose beginnings are poorly dated, held power. Ethiopian tradition credits King Lalibela (r. c. 1181 to 1221) with the eleven rock-hewn churches at the town now named after him. They were carved downward into soft volcanic rock, so each is a block freed from the living hillside; Bete Giyorgis is cut in the shape of a cross. Names in the complex, such as a stream called the Jordan, present it as a New Jerusalem. Some scholars link this to Saladin's capture of Jerusalem in 1187, but that is a hypothesis.

Archaeology complicates the tradition. Most specialists think the complex was cut in four or five phases between about the 7th and 13th centuries, and the archaeologist David Phillipson has argued that some parts began as fortified or residential buildings before becoming churches.

In 1270 Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe and founded the Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through their son Menelik I. That claim is set out in the Kebra Nagast ("Glory of the Kings"), compiled in Ge'ez around 1314 to 1322, according to its colophon by Yeshaq of Aksum and colleagues. It tells how the Queen of Sheba, called Makeda, visited Solomon and how Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. The colophon says it was translated from Arabic, itself from Coptic; scholars see a work that reshaped older material to legitimize a new line. Ethiopian emperors claimed Solomonic descent until Haile Selassie was deposed in 1974.

concepts.title: Kongo and Kanem-Bornu: Kings and World Religions
concepts.contentHtml:
The kingdom of Kongo, south of the lower Congo River, was centralized by the 15th century, with its capital at Mbanza Kongo in today's northern Angola. Portuguese ships under Diogo Cão arrived in 1483, and in 1491 King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized as João I. His son Mvemba a Nzinga, who ruled as Afonso I from about 1509 to 1542, made Catholicism a royal religion, founded schools and wrote to Lisbon in Portuguese.1 In letters of 1526 to João III of Portugal, Afonso complained that Portuguese merchants and their Kongolese partners were seizing free people, including nobles and members of his own family, and asked for priests and teachers rather than traders. He then appointed officials to check that people sold were lawfully enslaved. His aim was to control who could be enslaved and sold.

Kanem, northeast of Lake Chad, was ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty from at least the 11th century until 1846. Its king Hume (Humai) became a Muslim in the late 11th century. In the late 14th century pressure from the Bulala drove the court west of the lake to Bornu, where the walled capital Ngazargamu was built in the later 15th century. For Idris Alooma, who ruled in the late 16th century, his imam Ahmad ibn Furtu wrote a chronicle of the king's campaigns, a rare eyewitness account from inside the kingdom, which describes musketeers in his army. Bornu sent enslaved captives north across the Sahara to Fezzan and Tripoli.

In both kingdoms a world religion arrived with literacy, foreign allies and the pressures of the slave trade.
